messages.subject: Model Evaluation
parts:
Hi all

I'm trying to publish a paper where I model the distribution of fish in a Stream Network using Detection-Occupation models.

As Goodness of Fitness tests I compute a Bayesian p-value and I've calculated a posterior distribution of AUC as proposed by Zipikin et al. 2012:
http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1890/11-1936.1/abstract

However I have a reviewer proposing to evaluate the the model predicting ability against an independent data set. The reviewer advised to withhold a subset of the sites from the model construction and use it to evaluate the model performance.

Although this it's standard for other SDM methods (e. g.: Max Ent) I don't recall seen it in Detection-Occupation models. Does any one has some references of this?

Any help would be apreciated!

Cheers:
Mário

messages.author: 690b6056988a6321
messages.subject: RE: Model Evaluation
parts:
Hi Mario,

 

Our group has done this sort of thing in a couple of papers:

 

McCarthy, K. P., R. J. Fletcher, Jr., C. T. Rota, and R. L. Hutto.  2012.  Predicting species distributions from samples collected along roadsides.  Conservation Biology 26:68-77.

Rota, C. T., R. J. Fletcher, Jr., J. M. Evans, and R. L. Hutto. 2011. Does accounting for imperfect detection improve species distribution models?  Ecography 34: 659-670.

 

It is a bit tricky regarding how to deal appropriately with imperfect detection on the validation data, however. We tried a couple of ways in Rota et al, but I would imagine there are better ways to do so. I would imagine there are other papers out there as well (I think I have seen a few, but I don’t recall the citations off hand).

 

Hope that is helpful.

 

All the best,


Rob

I recently used cross-validation for model selection for occupancy models, and found it to be a good way to compare model performances. Although the paper describes the technique for multi-species models, it should be straightforward to apply the same methods to the single-species models.  (Cross-validation involves splitting the data into k subsets, withholding one at a time, and calculating a model performance statistic on each hold-out data set.)

Broms, K.M., M.B. Hooten, and R.M. Fitzpatrick. In press. Model selection and assessment for multi-species occupancy models.  Ecology.  DOI: 10.1890/15-1471.1

Cheers,

messages.subject: RE: Model Evaluation
parts:
Hi Mario,

 

I will let the Bayesian experts on the group answer your question, but I would say that the decision on holding out data depends a bit on the ultimate goal. If the goal is to understand how well a model predicts to unsampled locations, k-fold validation is useful, but prospective sampling (independent sampling of new locations or times) is better because the data are more independent than the data used for model building, leading to a more realistic assessment of the model to predict well in space or time. Also, in the SDM literature there has been some criticism of simple k-fold validation because it can result in folds that are not independent samples, leading to the selection of overly complex models (see Wegner and Olden 2012, Methods Ecol Evol, as an example). As a potential solution, some have advocated ‘block’ validation in regards to leaving data out, where entire geographic blocks are removed rather than a random sample points in the k-fold partition.

 

All the best,


Rob

HI Mario, 

The MCMC iterations provide an estimation of the posterior distributions given the data.  If each iteration were run on a different portion of the data, then you would no longer have the same interpretation of the chains.

The purpose of the k-fold validation is to mimic the more ideal setting of having an independent/ hold-out data set to test the models. If different data were selected for each iteration, it would no longer mimic the hold-out data set.  In machine learning, they often split their data into training (to build the models) and testing (to compare model performance). However, in ecology the data sets are usually smaller and there is not enough data to be comfortable completely withholding a large portion of the data when building the models.

The k-fold validation does require one to run the model k times, but with today's parallel processing and cloud servers, this is not as burdensome as it once was. I've been lucky to have department servers on which I run my models but a colleague of mine found Amazon's cluster computing to be invaluable for his dissertation (https://aws.amazon.com/hpc/). Also, you use the same exact BUGS/ JAGS code that has already been created when building the model. I find that I have to run the model so many times in my model building and testing, that the CV ends up not being as burdensome as the model building.

~Kristin

HI Mario, 

The MCMC iterations provide an estimation of the posterior distributions given the data.  If each iteration were run on a different portion of the data, then you would no longer have the same interpretation of the chains.

The purpose of the k-fold validation is to mimic the more ideal setting of having an independent/ hold-out data set to test the models. If different data were selected for each iteration, it would no longer mimic the hold-out data set.  In machine learning, they often split their data into training (to build the models) and testing (to compare model performance). However, in ecology the data sets are usually smaller and there is not enough data to be comfortable completely withholding a large portion of the data when building the models.

The k-fold validation does require one to run the model k times, but with today's parallel processing and cloud servers, this is not as burdensome as it once was. I've been lucky to have department servers on which I run my models but a colleague of mine found Amazon's cluster computing to be invaluable for his dissertation (https://aws.amazon.com/hpc/). Also, you use the same exact BUGS/ JAGS code that has already been created when building the model. I find that I have to run the model so many times in my model building and testing, that the CV ends up not being as burdensome as the model building.

~Kristin

Dear Mario,

 

The trouble with measuring predictive ability in species distribution models is that most or all typically used statistics (e.g., AUC) are no longer appropriate once you formally recognize measurement error, as does an occupancy model. Testing how well a model predicts the (error-prone) observations is not a very interesting way of measuring prediction success in my view. What you would like to do is measure how well the model is able to predict the true presence/absence state.

 

In this respect, perhaps the best test of predictive ability for occupancy models that I have seen was in a paper by Petr Keil (around 2013 or 2014): they used ebird data for highly surveyed quadrats to validate a model applied to some atlas data set. For the ebird data, they chose quadrats that were more than 20 times visited within a year, so for all reasonable values of detection probability they could assume that the presence/absence status was ascertained without error (note: the combined detection probability over 20 independent visits is >0.98 for a species with per-visit p of 0.2). Then, they had a data set with assumed known truth and could evaluate the predictive success of their model against it.

 

Best regards  --- Marc

Dear Mario,

 

I don’t think that your approach is wrong. It looks straightforward: you compare an observed response with what they model says this response should be. This has been done, I believe, for occupancy models by Rota et al. (http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1600-0587.2010.06433.x/abstract).

 

However, I just think that such a test is perhaps not very relevant when you have nondetection measurement error in your response and when your model formally acknowledges this, as is a hallmark of occ models. In this case, you would rather want to gauge the goodness of a model by how well it predicts the true presence/absence. This distinction has been made in the recent paper by Jose Lahoz Monfort (http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/geb.12138/abstract):
